newsitem.title: USA: Suburbs play role in success of US welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: Suburbs play role in success of US welfare reform.

text.p: The success of welfare reform will be determined in places like this sprawling suburb of high tech companies, massive warehouses and start-up firms 20 minutes by car from downtown Baltimore.

As states begin to implement the new welfare law, which calls for half of recipients to work by 2002 and limits most benefits to five years, experts expect booming suburbs across the nation to provide many of the jobs that will be needed.

That may come as a surprise to suburban businesses and residents congratulating themselves on escaping the social and economic problems of the inner cities. But simple math says they will be very much involved in the experiment.

While the nation's poor are concentrated in big cities, that is not where the job growth is. In six of the eight largest urban regions, more than two-thirds of new jobs created during the 1980s were in the suburbs.

"The suburbs may be thinking since the poor currently live in the city that's where they'll stay and if they're suffering it's not really going to affect the suburbs," said Claudia Coulton, professor at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland who has examined job creation and the poor. But she said, "The suburbs have to be part of the solution."

With no massive federal investment in the cities in sight, experts are looking to transportation, targeted tax breaks and regional economic strategies to tie city and suburb together. These suburbs near Baltimore-Washington International Airport typify the problems and possibilities ahead.

About half of Maryland's nearly 200,000 welfare recipients live in Baltimore. The city had a nine percent job-growth rate in the 1980s, while surrounding suburbs grew 36 percent. But the region around this airport exploded with 400 percent growth and employment is now near 150,000.

"This place is booming," said Neil Shpritz, executive director of the BWI Business Partnership Inc., as work proceeded on a major highway project near his office and huge signs advertised a new middle-class housing development.

But Shpritz says companies in the suburbs, ranging from defence contractors to warehouse operations, have a common complaint. "We hear it from employers all the time, 'I can't find workers at the right price'" for entry-level positions that make up about 15 percent of jobs here, he said.

A recent study for the state projected about 200 new entry-level jobs would be created in Baltimore this fiscal year, compared to nearly 3,000 in surrounding suburbs. But many inner city workers simply cannot get to outlying jobs.

Modern suburbs are designed for cars, roomy middle class lawns and sprawling business parks -- not poor people and public transit. The history of many suburbs, including some near Baltimore, is replete with zoning laws and citizen action designed to keep low-income housing out.
Some suburban businesses have had to set up their own transportation systems, calling public transit inadequate.

"Light rail doesn't start working until 11 a.m. on Sunday, we start operating at 5:30 a.m. We're lucky enough to have our own vans so we can go pick people up downtown," said Sandy Landstrom, general manager at BWI Airport Marriott.

Baltimore is one of five cities awarded federal grants under Bridges to Work, a programme to provide transportation to get inner city workers to outlying jobs. The Clinton administration hopes to expand the programme to 75 cities.

Transportation experiments are also underway in cities like Detroit, which lost 100,000 jobs in the 1980s while its suburbs gained more than 250,000. A national coalition of transportation, community and jobs groups formed this week.
Maryland officials are also making it easier for welfare recipients to own cars and recruiting businesses in suburbs with tax breaks and other incentives to hire the poor.

Mark Alan Hughes, vice president of Public/Private Ventures in Philadelphia, who helped create Bridges to Work, says cities may be overwhelmed by the welfare law and warns of a welfare "dust bowl" as people migrate to find jobs.

There are indications some states may seek to comply with the new law not by trying to create new jobs but by giving poor people money to move elsewhere. How many will seek out suburbs and whether they be welcome is an open question.

"The cities are seen as a bunch of misgoverned areas full of losers. The notion they (suburbs) are part of a common bond is very hard to sell," said Melvin Levin, professor at the University of Maryland.
